blocks.text: Not every message in MCP is a question waiting for an answer. Sometimes a server just needs to say something, a file changed, a long task made progress, a tool list grew, without expecting or wanting anything back. That is a notification, the quiet, one way sibling of the request and response pair, and learning to spot the difference is one of the more useful habits a client author can build.
1. What a Notification Is

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A sender sends a notification to a receiver

blocks.text: A notification is a JSON-RPC message with a method and, usually, a params object, sent without any id field at all. That missing id is not an oversight, it is the entire point, it tells the receiving side plainly that no response is coming and none is wanted.

Structurally a notification looks almost like a request with one piece removed, and that one missing piece changes everything about how it is handled, there is no pending table entry to create, no future to resolve, the message is simply acted on and then forgotten.

Because there is no id, there is also nothing to correlate a notification against later, it does not sit in any pending table, it does not time out, it either gets handled the moment it arrives or it is missed entirely if the receiver was not listening.
2. Why Notifications Have No id Field

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A notification has no id field

blocks.text: The id field exists for exactly one reason, to let a response find its way back to the request that caused it. A notification has no response coming, so there is nothing for an id to eventually be matched against, including one would just be a value that is generated, sent, and never used again.

Leaving id out is also what makes a message unambiguously a notification the moment it is parsed, a client never has to guess whether a reply is expected, the presence or absence of id settles the question immediately.

It also saves the sender the trouble of generating and tracking an id it would never use again, a small efficiency, but one that keeps the protocol's bookkeeping honest, ids exist only where they serve an actual purpose.
3. The Structural Difference From a Request

A request and a notification share the same method and params shape, the only structural difference is that one has an id and the other does not. That single field is what tells the receiving side whether it owes a response or not.
A quick way to remember it, requests ask and wait, notifications tell and move on, the id field is simply the visible artifact of that difference in the JSON.
4. When Notifications Are Used

Notifications show up whenever one side has information to share that does not correspond to anything the other side explicitly asked for right now, a resource changing on disk, a long running tool call making incremental progress, a list of available tools growing after a plugin loads, or simple log output a server wants surfaced to the user.

The common thread is timing, none of these events happen in response to a specific request being answered, they happen whenever they happen, and a notification is the mechanism built for exactly that kind of asynchronous, unsolicited communication.

A useful test is to ask whether the information being sent is something the receiver asked for a moment ago, if yes, it belongs in a response, if the information is simply arising on its own schedule, it belongs in a notification.

This also explains why notifications tend to cluster around change and progress, both are naturally ongoing rather than one shot, a resource can change many times, a task can progress many times, and each of those moments deserves its own small, unsolicited message.
5. Common Notification Types in MCP

MCP defines a handful of standard notification methods that cover the most common needs, progress updates, resource and list changes, logging, and cancellation. Each one has its own params shape, but all of them share the same no id, no response structure.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Notification method","Sent by","Purpose"],"rows":[["notifications/progress","either side","Report incremental progress on a long running request"],["notifications/resources/updated","server","A subscribed resource changed"],["notifications/resources/listChanged","server","The overall list of available resources changed"],["notifications/tools/listChanged","server","The overall list of available tools changed"],["notifications/message","server","Log output for the client to display"],["notifications/cancelled","either side","A previously sent request should be treated as cancelled"],["notifications/initialized","client","The client has finished processing the initialize response"]]}

blocks.text: None of these method names are arbitrary, the notifications prefix itself is a convention MCP uses consistently, so a client can often tell just from the method name alone, before even checking for an id, that it is looking at a one way message.
6. Progress Notifications

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A long-running tool sends a progress notification

blocks.text: When a request is expected to take a while, the caller can attach a progressToken to it, and the side doing the work sends periodic notifications/progress messages carrying that same token, along with a progress value and, optionally, a total and a human readable message.

A caller only receives progress notifications for a request if it opted in by attaching a progressToken in the first place, requests that do not include one simply never generate progress traffic, keeping quieter calls quiet.
7. Resource Update Notifications

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A changed resource triggers a resource update notification

blocks.text: A client that has subscribed to a specific resource, as covered when discussing resource subscriptions, receives a notifications/resources/updated message whenever that particular resource's content changes, telling it that a fresh read would return something different than last time.

This notification does not carry the new content itself, only the fact that something changed, the client is expected to issue a fresh resources/read if it actually wants to see the updated data, keeping the notification itself small and cheap to send.

Subscriptions and their update notifications only exist for servers that declared the resources subscribe capability during initialization, a server without that capability never sends this notification at all, since it never accepted a subscription to begin with.
8. List Changed Notifications

Separate from any single resource changing, the overall set of tools, resources, or prompts a server offers can itself change, a plugin loading a new tool at runtime is a good example. When that happens the server sends a listChanged notification for the relevant category, and a client that cares refreshes its cached list by calling the matching list method again.

Notice that this particular notification carries no params at all, the message itself is the entire signal, there is nothing more specific to say beyond "go look again," which keeps it about as small as a JSON-RPC message can be.
9. Cancellation Notifications

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A client sends a cancellation notification to the server

blocks.text: Either side can send notifications/cancelled to say that a previously issued request should be abandoned, carrying the id of the request being cancelled and, optionally, a reason. The side that receives it makes a best effort to stop the work and simply never sends a response for that id.

A subtlety worth remembering is that cancellation is advisory, not a hard guarantee, the side doing the work makes a best effort to stop, but a response that was already fully built and about to be sent may still arrive anyway, and the sender of the cancellation should be prepared to simply ignore it if it does.

Sending notifications/cancelled for a request id that has already completed and been responded to is harmless, the receiving side simply has nothing left to cancel and ignores it, which is why clients do not need to worry about racing a cancellation against a fast finishing request.
10. Logging Notifications

A server can send notifications/message to push log lines toward the client at a chosen severity level, debug, info, warning, or error among them, giving operators and developers visibility into what the server is doing without that visibility ever being tied to a specific request and response exchange.

A client is free to filter these by severity before showing anything to a user, treating notifications/message as raw material for its own logging pipeline rather than something that has to be displayed verbatim.
11. Notifications Flow in Both Directions

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Notifications flow from client to server and from server to client

blocks.text: It is easy to picture notifications as something only servers send, since resource changes and progress often originate on the server, but the direction is not fixed by the protocol, a client can send notifications too, cancellation and the initialized notification being the clearest examples of client to server traffic.
12. The initialized Notification After Handshake

Once a client receives the response to its initialize request, it sends back a notifications/initialized message, a one way signal that says, in effect, the handshake is complete and normal operation can begin. The server does not reply to it, and does not need to, it simply starts accepting ordinary requests from that point on.

Until this notification goes out, a server is technically still waiting for the handshake to close, some servers hold off on certain background behavior until they have seen it, treating it as the true starting gun for the session.

Some clients also use the moment right before sending this notification to do their own final setup, registering handlers for the notification types the server just declared support for during capability negotiation.
13. Notifications Are Fire and Forget

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A notification is fire and forget

blocks.text: Sending a notification is a one way action, the sender writes it to the transport and moves on, there is no future to await, no pending table entry to create, and no timeout to worry about because nothing was ever promised in return.

This also means a notification's sender has no built in way of knowing whether it was even processed successfully, the send itself either succeeds at the transport level or it does not, but the semantics of what the receiver actually did with it are invisible from the sending side.

blocks.title: No retries by default
blocks.content: Because there is no response, there is also no natural signal telling the sender a notification needs to be retried, if delivery reliability matters, that has to be built on top, not assumed from the protocol itself.

blocks.text: This is the same reason mailing a letter and making a phone call feel different, one is sent and trusted to arrive, the other waits on the line until the other person actually answers, notifications are the letter, requests are the phone call.
14. Why the Server Cannot Know If a Client Received a Notification

Because there is no response, there is also no acknowledgment, a server that sends notifications/resources/updated has no built in confirmation that the client actually processed it, only that the transport accepted the write. If a client happens to be disconnected at that exact moment, the notification is simply lost.

blocks.title: Notifications are best effort, not guaranteed delivery
blocks.content: Anything that truly must be known to have happened belongs in a request and response exchange, where the response itself is the guarantee. Notifications are for information that is helpful when it arrives but not catastrophic if it occasionally does not.

blocks.text: This is one more reason capability negotiation happens through a request and response handshake rather than through notifications, the initialize exchange needs a guaranteed reply, so it was deliberately built as a request, not a notification.
15. Notifications vs Requests Structurally

Side by side, a request commits its sender to waiting for something, and commits its receiver to eventually sending something back. A notification commits neither side to anything beyond the single message itself. That asymmetry in obligation is the real difference, the id field is just the visible marker of it.
16. Notifications and Retry Logic

Because a notification has no response, it also has nothing to retry against, if a client is unsure whether a critical notification actually reached the server, the only real fix is to redesign that piece of communication as a request instead, so that a response can serve as the acknowledgment.

This is a deliberate tradeoff, not a gap in the protocol, notifications are meant for information that loses little value if occasionally dropped, and anything more important than that should not have been modeled as a notification in the first place.

In practice this means an MCP implementation should audit its own notification usage occasionally, asking of each one, would it actually be a problem if this particular message were silently lost, if the honest answer is yes, that is a sign it was modeled the wrong way.
Worked Example
Trace what happens when a long running tools/call reports progress and then completes.

items: 1. Client sends tools/call with id 61 and params including a progressToken of "job-61".
2. Server begins work and, partway through, sends { jsonrpc: "2.0", method: "notifications/progress", params: { progressToken: "job-61", progress: 40, total: 100 } }.
3. Client receives this message, notices it has no id, routes it to its progress handler instead of its pending response table, and updates a progress bar to 40 percent.
4. Server sends one or two more progress notifications as work continues.
5. Server finishes and sends the actual response, { jsonrpc: "2.0", id: 61, result: { content: [ { type: "text", text: "Done" } ] } }.
6. Client matches id 61 against its pending table, resolves the waiting call, and the progress bar disappears in favor of the final result.

blocks.text: Common Mistakes

items: Trying to look up an incoming notification in the pending requests table by id, when it never had one to begin with.
Assuming a notification was successfully handled just because it was successfully sent, and building critical logic on that assumption.
Sending an id on a message that is meant to be a notification, which turns it into a request the other side now feels obligated to answer.
Ignoring notifications/cancelled and continuing to do expensive work the caller has already given up on.
Forgetting to send notifications/initialized after a successful handshake, leaving the server unsure whether the client considers setup complete.
Treating every server to client message as a notification, without checking for the id field that would mark it as an actual response.

blocks.text: Practice
Write a message router that inspects an incoming JSON-RPC message and dispatches it correctly, notifications to an event handler, and responses to a pending request resolver.
Key Takeaway

A notification is a request with the id field deliberately removed, and that one missing field changes everything, no response is expected, no response is sent, and the message is simply acted on and forgotten. They exist for anything asynchronous a server or client needs to share that was not asked for directly.
The next topic, Message IDs, looks more closely at that very field, what makes an id valid, who generates it, and exactly why it has to stay unique for as long as a request is still pending.
